deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page is Gauss's working log of the first meridian observations with the new Repsold meridian circle at the Göttingen observatory, 20-23 April 1818. Each row gives four things:
- T: the transit time on the sidereal clock.
- R: the circle reading, a signed zenith distance. It is + for stars south of the zenith and − for north-side stars, which here are all observed in lower culmination.
- the apparent place from the tables (α, δ) for the reference stars.
- r: the refraction, followed by a derived quantity φ' = 51°40'+x.
Barometer and thermometer readings (Paris inches and lines; Réaumur) bracket each session, e.g. 27z6l1, +6.2°. The final '+4.4 || +0.5' probably gives an inner and an outer thermometer.

1. ZENITH POINT / LATITUDE+INDEX (rightmost column).
For a south star: φ' = R + r + δ.
For a north star in lower culmination: φ' = 180° − δ − (|R| + r).
Here φ' = φ + c, where c is the index (zenith-point) error of the circle, about +9' since φ ≈ 51°31'48". The checks below are my own.
- Sirius (20 Apr): 68°7'8.0" + 142.4" − 16°28'32.1" = 51°40'58.3". Matches '58.3'.
- Regulus: 38°48'57.7" + 46.3" + 12°51'10.6" = 51°40'54.6". Matches '54.6'. This requires the refraction to read 46.3, not 46.7.
- Polaris (lower culmination, table δ = 88°20'12.4"): R = −39°57'63.4" = −39°58'3.4", r = 48.7". Then 180° − 88°20'12.4" − 39°58'52.1" = 51°40'55.5". Matches '55.5'.
- α Cygni (22 Apr): 7°2'59.7" + 7.0" + 44°37'41.93" = 51°40'48.6". Matches '48.6'.
- Vesta (worked out on the previous page): ZD = 46°19'37.2" + 61.1" = 46°20'38.3". Then δ = 51°40'55.5" − 46°20'38.2" = +5°20'17.3".
The other stars serve as refraction and zenith-point material:
- '32.6.43,7' must be 52°6'43.7". Refraction 74.5" belongs to ZD ≈ 52°, and that reading gives δ(γ Vir, 1818) ≈ −0°28'.
- 'ε', κ and η Cas are lower culminations at clock 11h59, 12h22 and 12h38. The first fits β Cas (RA 1818 ≈ 23h59.6m, δ ≈ 58°8'): |R| + c + r ≈ 70°18.5', giving δ ≈ 58°9.6'.
- Polaris was likewise observed in lower culmination at clock 12h55m13.67s. Its upper-culmination RA is 0h55m33.49s.

2. CLOCK RATE.
Sirius gives T = 6h37m12.57s (20 Apr), 14.61s (22 Apr), 15.93s (23 Apr).
(14.61 − 12.57)/2 = 1.02 s/day, so the clock gains about 1 s per sidereal day. Gauss writes 'Gang der Uhr +1.00'.

3. TRANSIT REDUCTION (the substantive part).
Gauss writes the reduction of clock time to right ascension for 20 Apr 6h37m in Bessel's three-constant form:
α = T + K + n·tanδ + c·secδ, with K = −1.28 s, n = +2.90 s, c = −3.41 s.
He then splits K = −1.28 into two parts:
- the clock behind ('Uhr [zurück] 2.37'), i.e. clock correction +2.37 s;
- an instrumental reduction to the true meridian, m = −3.65 s.
This gives 'Red. der Durchg.Z. auf den wahren Meridian: −3.65 + 2.90 tanδ − 3.41 secδ'.
The constants come from fitting the fundamental stars. Polaris, with tanδ ≈ secδ ≈ 34.4, is in practice what separates n from c.
For lower culmination the rule (mine) is δ → 180° − δ, which changes the signs of tanδ and secδ.
My check, applying a rate of 1 s/day from the Sirius epoch:
- Sirius: −1.28 − 0.857 − 3.556 = −5.69 → 6.88 vs table 7.01 (+0.13).
- Regulus: −4.12, rate −0.14 → 40.81 vs 40.88 (+0.07).
- Spica (δ ≈ −10°12'): −5.27, rate −0.28 → 38.28 vs 38.24 (−0.04).
- α Cyg: −3.21, rate −2.6 → 12.5 vs 13.24 (+0.7).
- Polaris (lower culmination): +16.34, rate −0.26 → 29.75 vs 33.49 (+3.7 s, i.e. about 1.6" of great circle).
A three-star solution reproduces the constants only roughly: Sirius+Regulus+Polaris gives n ≈ 2.5, c ≈ −3.1. Gauss probably also used the level (Libelle) readings for the axis inclination, which links m and n via φ. The level readings are pivots inward +0°9'31.7" and outward 0°9'37.7" on 21 Apr at 3h p.m., i.e. an inclination term of about 3".
The previous page applies the formula to Vesta: 13h19m14.87s − 0.28 (rate) − 1.28 + [n tanδ] − 3.42 = 13h19m9.92s.
errors: The previous page's Vesta reduction uses +0.03 s for the n·tanδ term. With n = 2.90 and δ = +5°20'17" this term should be about +0.27 s; the stated total 13h19m9.92s is consistent with the 0.03. Either it is a slip (RA too small by about 0.24 s) or the transcription of that page is wrong.

The residuals of α Cygni (about +0.7 s) and Polaris (about +3.7 s in time, about 1.6" of arc) are not reproduced exactly with the stated constants. The constants are probably a compromise fit that includes level data, or the tabular places are uncertain. This is not a clear error.
The refraction entered for the first Cassiopeia star (141.7") is too small for ZD ≈ 70.3°: neighbouring entries give about 160". It is probably 161.7 or a misreading.
'32.6.43,7' for γ Virginis must be 52°6'43.7". This is a slip of pen or a misreading; the 74.5" refraction confirms ZD ≈ 52°.

results.what: Reduction of meridian transit times to right ascension in the form α = T + m + n tanδ + c secδ, with constants m, n, c determined from fundamental stars including Polaris in lower culmination (rule δ → 180°−δ)
results.modern_name: Bessel's transit-instrument formula (equivalent to Tobias Mayer's formula)
results.usually_credited_to: T. Mayer (1750s) for the error decomposition; F. W. Bessel (Königsberg, c. 1820s) for the m + n tanδ + c secδ form

results.what: Determination of latitude + index error (zenith point) from circle readings plus refraction for southern stars and lower-culminating circumpolars
results.modern_name: Zenith-point / latitude determination with a meridian circle
results.usually_credited_to: standard practice (Bradley, Piazzi, Bessel, Reichenbach-circle users)

results.what: Clock rate from repeated Sirius transits: +1.00 s/day

results.usually_credited_to: routine; Gauss's Göttingen observations of Vesta are known

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine observatory reduction work. It records the first use of Gauss's Repsold meridian circle in April 1818, which is historically known. The only mildly notable point is that Gauss already writes the transit correction in the m + n tanδ + c secδ form in 1818. That form follows trivially from Mayer's formula and was in contemporary use, so it is not a discovery.

checkable.asserts: Reduced Sirius clock seconds ≈ 6.88, vs tabular RA seconds 7.01
Polaris lower culmination reduced seconds ≈ 29.75, vs 33.49 (residual ≈ 3.7 s)
Instrumental constant plus clock correction equals the combined constant −1.28
Clock rate ≈ 1.02 s/day, which Gauss rounds to +1.00
The n·tanδ term for Vesta is ≈ 0.27 s, not 0.03 s

transcription_corrections: Title: 'Erste Beobachtungen mit Repsolds Kreise' is correct.
Regulus refraction reads 46,3 (not 46,7); the φ' value 54.6 requires 46.3.
The γ Virginis circle reading should be +52°6'43.7" (not 32°): it is consistent with refraction 74.5" and with δ(γ Vir, 1818) ≈ −0°28'.
'ε Cassiop' is very probably β Cassiopeiae: lower culmination at clock 11h59, RA(1818) ≈ 23h59.6m, the derived δ ≈ 58°9.6' matches β Cas. It may be Gauss's own label.
The first Cassiopeia star's refraction is probably 161,7 rather than 141,7.

The Polaris transit is at clock 12h55m13.67s (lower culmination), not 0h55m. The overwritten entry in the δ column is 88°20'12.4". The values 57.4/58.8 above and below the circle reading are probably separate microscope or reading values around 39°57'58".
The Spica clock time is overwritten; the final value is 13h15m43.83s. The circle reading is ≈ +61°51'.
The April 21 level reading 'Spitzen nach aussen' is 0°9'37.7"; '(3u N.M.)' means 3 Uhr Nachmittags.
In 'zu eben der Zeit also Uhr [zurück] 2"37', 'zurück' is struck through.
